original_question: Find a class of nonnegative majorants mu in C[-1, 1] for which the associated degree-n snake polynomial has a Chebyshev expansion of the first kind whose coefficients are either all nonnegative or sign-alternating.
target_in_paper: Section 7 (Snake Polynomials), Problem 7.1, with nearby context from Conjecture 7.1 and Theorem 7.3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the actual open problem’s core objects and property: nonnegative majorants μ on [-1,1], the associated degree-n snake polynomial, and the question of when its Chebyshev expansion of the first kind has coefficients that are either all nonnegative or sign-alternating. It also stays at the right scope: it asks for a class of majorants, which matches Problem 7.1 rather than the narrower special case in Conjecture 7.1.
missing_details: The official target is Problem 7.1 in Section 7, not the narrower Conjecture 7.1; the draft does not say this explicitly.
The ambient polynomial space should be specified: P_n, the real algebraic polynomials of degree at most n.

The snake polynomial should be defined stand-alone: for a given n and majorant μ, it is the n-th snake polynomial associated with μ, characterized by the majorization condition on [-1,1] together with n+1 alternating contact points with ±μ.
The existence condition is implicit in the paper: one assumes there exists a nonzero polynomial p in P_n with |p(x)| ≤ μ(x) on [-1,1], so that the associated snake polynomial exists.
The snake polynomial is unique only up to orientation (global sign); this matters when formulating coefficient sign conditions.

The quantifier over n is missing. Problem 7.1 is naturally about the class of majorants for which the associated n-th snake polynomials have the stated Chebyshev-sign property, not just one fixed unnamed degree.
The Chebyshev expansion should be written explicitly, e.g. ω_{μ,n}(x)=Σ_{j=0}^n a_j T_j(x).

The phrase "sign-alternating" should be made explicit in a stand-alone formulation; because of orientation ambiguity, one should say that after choosing an orientation of ω_{μ,n}, either a_j ≥ 0 for all j or (-1)^j a_j ≥ 0 for all j.

Your draft adds μ in C[-1,1]. Section 7’s Problem 7.1 is stated for "majorants" in general, while continuity appears explicitly in the narrower Conjecture 7.1; this distinction should be made clear if one wants paper-faithfulness.

The motivation from Theorem 7.3 is implicit in the draft: this coefficient-sign property is important because it implies extremality of the snake polynomial for the corresponding Markov- and Duffin-Schaeffer-type inequalities.
refined_question: Let P_n denote the real algebraic polynomials of degree at most n. For a nonnegative majorant μ:[-1,1]→[0,∞) and an integer n≥1, assume there exists a nonzero polynomial p∈P_n such that |p(x)|≤μ(x) on [-1,1], and let ω_{μ,n}∈P_n be the corresponding n-th snake polynomial, unique up to sign, characterized by |ω_{μ,n}(x)|≤μ(x) on [-1,1] and by the existence of alternation points τ_0^*>⋯>τ_n^* in [-1,1] with ω_{μ,n}(τ_i^*)=(-1)^i μ(τ_i^*). Determine classes of such majorants μ for which, for every n for which ω_{μ,n} exists, one can choose the orientation of ω_{μ,n} so that its Chebyshev expansion of the first kind, ω_{μ,n}(x)=Σ_{j=0}^n a_j T_j(x), has either a_j≥0 for all j or (-1)^j a_j≥0 for all j.
justification: The draft is closest to Section 7, Problem 7.1, which asks for classes of majorants whose associated snake polynomials have nonnegative or sign-alternating Chebyshev expansions. It is not closest to Conjecture 7.1, because your wording asks to "find a class" rather than to prove the specific even-convex case. The nearby Section 7 context defines the n-th snake polynomial and its alternation-point characterization, while Theorem 7.3 explains why this coefficient-sign condition matters: it yields extremality in the corresponding Markov- and Duffin-Schaeffer-type inequalities. The refined version therefore keeps the exact scope of Problem 7.1 and only adds the notation, existence hypothesis, orientation issue, and an explicit coefficient-sign convention needed to make the question stand alone.
